title: Affect Theory
keyWorks: B. Massumi, Parables for the Virtual (2002)
S. Ahmed, The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004)
S. Ahmed, The Promise of Happiness (2010)
S. Ahmed, Living a Feminist Life (2017)
summary: Affect theory is a strand of humanities thought from the 1990s–2010s that grew out of the philosophy of Spinoza and Deleuze. It looks at feelings not as something locked “inside” a person but as forces that pass through bodies, between people and through society. Brian Massumi studies affect as bodily intensity, while Sara Ahmed studies how emotions circulate and “stick” to people, things and words.
onEmotions: Massumi distinguishes affect from emotion. Affect is a pre-personal intensity: a bodily surge that happens before we have time to name it. Emotion is intensity that has already been “captured,” given a name and a place in the story we tell about ourselves. Sara Ahmed asks a different question: not “what is an emotion?” but “what do emotions do?” In her view, emotions do not belong to one person: they move between people, “stick” to objects, groups and words, and in doing so draw boundaries — who “we” are, who “they” are, what counts as a good life. For both, a feeling is neither a malfunction nor a purely private matter but a way in which the world touches us and we touch the world.

anxiety.text: In the 2000s Americans woke up every morning to the color of the “terror threat level” — yellow, orange, red. Brian Massumi analyzed this scale as an example of how a danger that has not yet happened is already acting on the body now. If anxiety lives in you too, there is nothing shameful in that. Massumi calls such a threat an “affective fact” — a future that is felt as real in the present. The body responds to such signals before we have time to think them through, and anxiety becomes the general background of an era, not just your personal trait. This distinction can be a little freeing: anxiety passes through you the way weather passes through a city, but it does not exhaust who you are. And its intensity, for Massumi, is also an unformed energy that can find another channel.
anxiety.practice: Place your hand where anxiety lives in your body right now and ask yourself: what in this minute — not in the future — is it responding to?

fear.text: Shoulders tighten, steps get shorter, certain streets quietly vanish from your personal map — this, for Sara Ahmed, is how fear makes the body smaller. It is an ancient and necessary signal, and it deserves respect. Massumi emphasizes that fear happens first in the body: breath, muscles and heart react a split second before the thought “I’m afraid” appears. Ahmed adds a social dimension to this. And this shrinking is unevenly distributed: some are told from childhood “be careful,” others “the world is yours.” Seeing this means understanding that your fear is not only a personal weakness but also a trace of how the world has treated people like you. Then you can gently ask yourself what space fear has taken from you, and reclaim at least a small part of it.
fear.practice: Picture one place or activity that fear has trained you out of, and in your mind take the smallest, safest step back toward it. Notice how your body answers.

quote.text: The skin is faster than the word.
quote.author: Brian Massumi

sadness.text: “Come on, smile!” — a sad person hears this so often that they start apologizing for their own face. Your sadness doesn’t need to apologize. In The Promise of Happiness, Sara Ahmed shows how society turns happiness into a duty: we are expected to be glad about the “right” things, and a sad person is seen as a problem to be fixed as quickly as possible. Ahmed suggests not rushing into such fixing. Unhappiness, in her view, can be a form of knowledge: sadness sometimes notices what general cheerfulness prefers not to see — injustice, loss, what doesn’t “add up” in life. Seen this way, your sadness is not a breakdown of mood but a sensitivity that is registering something. You can stay with it without hurrying to turn it into a smile, and listen to what it is saying.
sadness.practice: Say quietly: “Maybe my sadness is noticing that…” — and finish the sentence. Don’t fix anything, just listen.

grief.text: A word is always smaller than what it names — Brian Massumi builds his theory of intensity on this. In grief it is especially clear: no timeline and no right words can hold what is happening to you. The word “grief” only partly captures what is happening in the body — the heaviness, the emptiness in the chest, the sudden waves. So it’s all right if you cannot explain it. Sara Ahmed, drawing on Judith Butler, points out that society does not recognize all losses equally: some are mourned publicly, while others go unnoticed — for example, the loss of a friend, an animal, or a relationship that those around you did not consider “real.” Your grief is real even if no one around you has confirmed it. It is evidence of a bond that mattered and still matters.
grief.practice: Name — to yourself or on paper — what you have lost, the way you feel it, not the way people usually talk about it.

loneliness.text: There are rooms where the chairs seem to have been set out for someone else — Sara Ahmed describes this feeling with almost physical precision. Loneliness hurts, and that pain says how much we need others. Ahmed invites us to see feelings not as something locked inside an individual: emotions arise at the boundary between us and the world, and they themselves draw that boundary. In Queer Phenomenology she writes that space can be arranged “for” some bodies and not others — and then a person feels out of place, as if the world does not reach out to meet them. Loneliness is not proof that something is wrong with you but sometimes a sign that there are few shapes around you that you fit into. Ahmed also reminds us of something else: those who feel “out of line” often find one another, and such a meeting changes the space itself.
loneliness.practice: Go out for a little while where there are people — a park, a café, a shop — and look for those who also seem “out of line.” Just notice: you are not the only ones.

quote.text: Emotions are not simply “in” the individual or the social, but produce the very surfaces and boundaries that allow the individual and the social to be delineated as if they are objects.
quote.author: Sara Ahmed

anger.text: A family dinner, everyone smiling, and one person says: “That hurt me.” It is this person who is immediately treated as the cause of the spoiled mood — Sara Ahmed called them the “feminist killjoy.” Your anger may come from the same place: it is responding to something truly unjust. Ahmed puts it this way: when you point out a problem, you become the problem. Her point is not that anger is always good but that anger often carries information others find uncomfortable to hear. This can relieve you of unnecessary guilt for “ruining the atmosphere.” Your anger is not necessarily destruction; sometimes it is a way of saying “something is wrong here” and refusing to pretend that everything is fine.
anger.practice: Ask your anger: what exactly is it pointing to — and what would you like others to finally hear?

quote.text: Does the feminist kill other people’s joy by pointing out moments of sexism? Or does she expose the bad feelings that get hidden, displaced, or negated under public signs of joy?
quote.author: Sara Ahmed

shame.text: “Before whom?” Sara Ahmed would first ask your shame. You want to disappear, to hide your face — one of the most tormenting feelings. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion she shows that shame is always bound up with others. We feel ashamed before someone’s gaze — real or imagined — and we are ashamed because we have fallen short of an ideal that matters to us and to those whose love we want to keep. Shame, for Ahmed, turns the self against itself: the gaze turns inward, the body seems to shrink. But there is consolation in this description too: shame shows how deeply you value your connection with people and their recognition. You can ask yourself whose ideal this is and whether it is really yours. Sometimes shame simply reports that you have ended up outside someone else’s norm — not that you are a bad person.
shame.practice: Imagine that someone who regards you with kindness is looking at you right now. Stay under that gaze for a minute: what do they see?

guilt.text: When governments make public apologies, Sara Ahmed asks: to whom does attention finally return — to those who were harmed, or to those apologizing? Extending her thought, your guilt is a painful but very human feeling: you care how your actions have affected others. Ahmed notices a trap here: admitting guilt sometimes becomes a way of feeling good about ourselves again, and attention returns to the one who is guilty rather than to the one who was harmed. Hence a gentle conclusion: endlessly punishing yourself is not the same as repairing a relationship. Guilt “sticks” and can spread far beyond the act itself. It can be brought back to its real size: what exactly happened, whom it affected, and what is actually possible to do now.
guilt.practice: Tell yourself out loud, in two sentences, what exactly happened — without judging. Then name one small step directed toward the other person rather than toward punishing yourself.

envy.text: A house with a porch, a wedding photo, the right career, the right body — in The Promise of Happiness Sara Ahmed calls such things “happy objects”: culture tells us in advance what is supposed to make us happy. Ahmed hardly writes about envy directly, but extending her thought, this unpleasant feeling tells a lot about you. These objects carry a promise, and we reach for them without even choosing. And in “affective economies,” for Ahmed, feelings accumulate value as they circulate: the more often the image of a “happy life” flashes before our eyes, the stronger its pull. Your envy is not a vice but a trace of these promises. You can examine it: what do you actually want, and what has been promised to you from outside?
envy.practice: Write down what you envy right now, and next to it what promise you think is hidden in this “object.” Does it sound like your own desire?

emptiness.text: “The problem that has no name” — that is what Betty Friedan in 1963 called the emptiness felt by perfectly comfortable housewives. Sara Ahmed returns to this phrase in The Promise of Happiness, and it may fit your heaviness too, for which there seems to be “no reason.” Women in the mid-20th century lived the life that was considered happy — home, family, prosperity — and felt a strange emptiness inside. Ahmed sees this not as a personal defect but as a sign that the promise of happiness invested in the “right” life had not worked. Your emptiness can be an honest response to a life running on someone else’s script. In Massumi’s spirit, one can add: even in an apparent lull, the body keeps sensing — intensity doesn’t disappear completely, it just hasn’t found words yet. Emptiness is not the end of feeling but a pause in it.
emptiness.practice: Notice one tiny sensation in your body right now — the warmth of your palms, the ground under your feet. Simply note that it is there.

confusion.text: Your hand reaches for a light switch that is no longer there — a glitch familiar after any move. In Queer Phenomenology Sara Ahmed calls such moments disorientation, and your confusion is their larger version: the ground slips away, and it’s unclear where to go. When the familiar lines along which life moves suddenly stop holding, the body loses its footing, and for a while the world seems “askew.” Ahmed is in no hurry to regard this as only a misfortune: disorientation shows that our directions were not natural — they were formed by repetition, habits, other people’s expectations. In such moments it becomes visible that you could turn another way. That doesn’t make confusion pleasant. But it can be lived as a transitional state in which new directions open up, rather than as proof that you have “lost your way.”
confusion.practice: Stand up and slowly turn a full circle where you are, naming to yourself what you see on each side. Disorientation is also a chance to see the room from an unfamiliar angle.

fatigue.text: A twig that has been bending for a long time one day breaks with a dry crack — Sara Ahmed calls this moment a snap and reminds us that everyone hears the crack, while no one sees the long pressure before it. Burnout is not laziness or weakness of character. In Living a Feminist Life she writes about how wearing it is to keep coming up against “brick walls” — obstacles visible only to those who run into them. Pressure builds up unnoticed, and a breakdown that looks sudden is in fact the result of long strain. Ahmed also rethinks self-care, drawing on the poet Audre Lorde: for those whom the world depletes, self-care is not a whim but a way to survive and keep going. Your tiredness is a meaningful response to the load. Rest here is not a reward for results but a condition for remaining yourself.
fatigue.practice: Lie down or sit so that your body has nothing to hold up, and do nothing for five minutes. This isn’t a reward for results but a condition for remaining yourself.

quote.text: Caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation, and that is an act of political warfare.
quote.author: Audre Lorde

boredom.text: A microshock is Massumi’s name for a tiny shift of attention: the light flickers, a door creaks, the rhythm of your breathing changes. Every minute holds dozens of them, but boredom, which can be truly oppressive, seems to muffle them all: time drags, everything looks flat. Affect, following Spinoza and Deleuze, is the capacity to affect and to be affected. Boredom resembles a state in which this capacity has temporarily narrowed: the world keeps touching us, but the touches don’t get through. Microshocks make up every moment of perception. They are there now too: a change in the light, a sound, your own breathing. Boredom in this light is not the emptiness of the world but a muffling of contact with it. It doesn’t have to be drowned out with new stimuli; sometimes it is enough to notice, a little more slowly, what is already happening.
boredom.practice: For one minute, become a “collector of microshocks”: note the three smallest changes around you — a sound, a movement, a shift in the light.

joy.text: “A passage to a greater perfection” — that is how Spinoza defined joy, and his heir Brian Massumi understands it as the moment when the capacity to act and feel expands and the body seems to grow larger. Such joy doesn’t need to be earned or justified: it happens. Sara Ahmed, while criticizing the “duty to be happy,” is not at all against joy. She reminds us that the English word happiness comes from hap — “chance,” “luck”: happiness was originally connected with what simply befalls us, not with living rightly according to plan. Ahmed suggests giving happiness back this element of chance. So your joy doesn’t have to be built into a grand story of success. You can simply let it be — like an unexpected gift of the moment.
joy.practice: Tell someone in one sentence what “happened” to you today and brought joy — as a small event of the day.

love.text: To affect and to be affected — that is how Massumi, following Spinoza, defines affect, and in love the formula becomes almost tangible. The tenderness you feel makes you both stronger and more vulnerable. Love is one of the forms in which this capacity flourishes: another person begins to change your rhythm, your breathing, your thoughts. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed stresses that love is not only a private feeling: it orients us, turns us toward someone, and out of it a “we” is formed. Ahmed soberly notes that this “we” is sometimes built by excluding others. But the capacity to love itself is how the world becomes shared. You can accept your tenderness not as weakness but as a sign of openness: your boundaries are mobile and alive.
love.practice: Think of the person you love and notice what changes in your body — posture, voice, the pace of your breath. Name it to yourself in one word.

gratitude.text: “Say thank you!” — many of us learned gratitude on command with this phrase as children. Your gratitude now seems different: a warm feeling in which you notice that someone or something has supported you. Gratitude, for Ahmed, like other emotions, circulates: it passes from person to person, connects, makes bonds visible. But Ahmed also teaches attentiveness: in The Promise of Happiness she shows how certain people — migrants, for example — are expected to have the “right” feelings: to be happy and content with what they have been given. Gratitude that is demanded stops being gratitude and becomes a debt. So it is worth distinguishing: is your gratitude alive and free — or do you feel obliged to feel it? Real gratitude does not cancel the right to see what was wrong as well. It can live alongside other feelings without crowding them out.
gratitude.practice: Name one thing you are grateful for without any effort — and one thing you are more or less expected to be grateful for.

hope.text: A “margin of maneuverability” is what Brian Massumi calls the tiny space that exists even in the tightest situation: a place where the next step can be taken slightly differently. Your hope is a quiet strength, and Massumi proposes separating it from the expectation of success. If you hope only for a big goal or a guaranteed result, hope becomes fragile: any failure brings it down. Massumi looks for hope in the present — in that very margin. Hope in this sense is neither a forecast nor optimism but a feeling of openness, a sense that the situation is not yet finished. This is a relief: you don’t have to believe that everything will definitely be fine in order to feel that something is possible right now.
hope.practice: Do one habitual thing slightly differently today — by another route, in another order, with other words. That is a “margin of maneuverability” in miniature.

nostalgia.text: “Stickiness” is one of Sara Ahmed’s key words: feelings, in her view, stick to things and stay on them for years. Nostalgia is sweet and aching at once, and there is nothing naive about it. A smell, a melody, an old photograph become “sticky” with the feelings associated with them and, years later, bring them back whole. In Massumi’s spirit one can add that this memory lives in the body before it lives in words: the body recognizes a familiar intonation faster than we can recall where it comes from. Ahmed also notes that nostalgia can be collective — for the “good old days,” which were not good for everyone. But personal nostalgia above all shows what has stuck to you and what shaped you. You can accept it as a gentle touch of the past, without demanding that the past return.
nostalgia.practice: What smell, sound or object “sticks” most strongly to your past? Stay with this image for a minute and notice what it awakens in you.

quote.text: Affect is what sticks, or what sustains or preserves the connection between ideas, values, and objects.
quote.author: Sara Ahmed

craving.text: In the experiments Massumi cites, the brain launched a movement about half a second before the person “decided” on it. When a sharp craving hits — for a cigarette, a drink, your phone — it feels as if the decision has already been made for you: hard, but nothing to be ashamed of. Massumi calls this the “missing half-second.” Affect is always a little ahead of thought. Sara Ahmed adds in Queer Phenomenology that our actions are largely shaped by what is “within reach” — what the body is used to reaching for. A craving is not a verdict on your character but a bodily impulse laid down by repetition. But an impulse is not yet an act. Between the wave and the action you can create a tiny gap, and by changing what is within reach you can change the very direction of movement. The wave rises and falls.
craving.practice: Move the object of the craving at least a couple of meters away — into another room, into a drawer. Notice how the wave changes when it isn’t within reach.

addiction.text: A path walked every day becomes ever more visible, while one no one walks grows over — Sara Ahmed develops this image in What’s the Use? (2019). When life has been built around one thing for years, getting out of the circle is very hard, and it is not a moral weakness. Ahmed applies this idea to habits and institutions: use lays down direction. Addiction is a very well-trodden path along which the body and feelings go almost by themselves. This explains why leaving it is so hard — and lifts some of the shame. But Ahmed also talks about “desire lines”: paths people tread themselves, bypassing the official routes. A new path is laid down gradually — step by step, and often together with others.
addiction.practice: Name one small “new path” — a walk, a call, a short task — that you could walk today. If you like, you can walk it together with someone who understands, for example in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: A vague shame looks for something to stick to, and by morning, to extend Sara Ahmed’s thought, it finds any scrap of memory. Heaviness in the body, anxiety, gaps in memory: an uncomfortable state, but not one that makes you a bad person. Massumi emphasizes that the body registers more than the mind has time to grasp: intensities leave a trace even when they have no words. That is why in the morning anxiety can be stronger than the “facts” warrant — the body has not yet recovered. Ahmed would call such feelings “sticky”: they inflate whatever they cling to. Part of the morning dread is not knowledge about last night but affect looking for something to stick to. You can notice it without taking it on faith. First, take care of your body. Later, when it is calmer, your view of last night will be calmer too.
hangover.practice: Notice where in your body anxiety and shame are sitting right now, and tell yourself: “This is a state of the body, not a final verdict.” Then splash your face with cool water and breathe out slowly.

euphoria.text: The “virtual,” for Massumi, is not the unreal but a field of the possible that sometimes becomes tangible for a moment. When everything suddenly seems possible, you seem to be touching exactly that, and you can enjoy this vivid experience. Massumi, following Spinoza, describes affect as an increase or decrease in the capacity to act. Euphoria is a moment of sharp increase: the body seems to grow larger, and the world opens up with possibilities. Not all possibilities will be realized, but that doesn’t make the feeling false: you really did feel how much wider your life could be. Euphoria need neither be held on to nor immediately turned into decisions. You can simply live it and remember it as knowledge that openness is possible. When the high subsides, that knowledge will stay with you.
euphoria.practice: Stand for a minute with your shoulders open and your palms spread, and feel how much “larger” your body has become. Remember this sensation — it will be useful when the wave recedes.

crash.text: Intensity can’t last long, Massumi reminds us: it flares up and dissipates, and the body returns to its usual rhythm. After a celebration, a success or a vivid evening this dip can be bitter — as if everything has faded. In The Promise of Happiness, Sara Ahmed writes about “happy objects” — holidays, achievements, events that promise joy in advance. When the event is over, what remains is not only tiredness but also the gap between the promise and what is left afterward. The “comedown” is neither proof that the joy was fake nor a sign that you are broken. It is the natural movement of an affect that has ebbed. The dip doesn’t need to be urgently filled with a new high. You can let your body rest from the intensity.
crash.practice: Name one small, quiet thing that will support your body today: sleep, food, a warm shower. Do it without guilt.

panic.text: The body gets there before words — this is perhaps Brian Massumi’s central idea, and in a panic attack you feel it literally. Your heart pounds, your breath catches, it seems something irreversible is about to happen — it is genuinely frightening. In the body everything happens before thought: heart, breath and muscles react a split second before the word “fear” appears. Massumi also writes about how a threat that has not yet happened can feel completely real in the body. Panic is a wave of intensity that seizes the body faster than the mind can name it. That is why what helps is not arguing with your thoughts but turning to the body — in its own language. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. While it lasts, the body can be supported with breath and grounding, the way you would support a friend.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Name out loud three things you see, two you hear, and one you feel on your skin.

dread.text: Fear knows its object, while anxiety slides: Sara Ahmed describes how it jumps from the future to death, from death to meaninglessness. Existential dread — “what is it all for,” the sense of finitude and of the abyss — is a heavy experience, and you are not alone in it. Dread may be anxiety in its widest form — stuck to everything at once. Massumi, for his part, says that every moment holds an excess — life is more than what we manage to live and name in it. The abyss you feel is precisely this excess, which does not fit into an answer. It can be frightening, but it also means that life is not exhausted and that something in it always remains open.
dread.practice: Notice what your dread has “stuck” to right now. Then find one sensation that is happening right now — warmth, a sound, your breath — and stay with it for a minute.

fomo.text: The feed looks like a map with the points of happiness marked on it: the right party here, the right holiday there. The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you are not where you should be grows out of maps like this, and it is painful. Sara Ahmed reminds us that the English word happiness comes from hap — “chance,” “what happens.” But culture has turned happiness into a route: the right places, the right parties, the right life. Ahmed calls them “happiness scripts”: they make those who don’t follow them feel “out of place.” The fear of missing out is not your failure but an effect of a script that promises happiness happens somewhere out there. But if you give happiness back its “hap,” it turns out it can happen anywhere — including where you are now.
fomo.practice: Notice one small thing that “happened” to you today — a meeting, a taste, the light. It wasn’t part of any script.

sleepless.text: Three in the morning: anxiety was just clinging to work, now it’s on to health, then relationships. Sara Ahmed calls it “sticky”: it jumps from object to object, and without the day’s tasks this circling is especially noticeable. When you can’t sleep, everything seems more hopeless in the dark. Massumi emphasizes that affect lives in the body: even when thoughts seem endless, this is above all the state of an aroused organism. Night thoughts are not an insight about life but anxiety looking for something to stick to. It doesn’t need to be resolved with logic at three in the morning. You can turn to the body — breath, warmth, heaviness — and let it slowly calm down.
sleepless.practice: Notice what the anxiety is sticking to now and say inwardly: “There it is again.” Then slowly feel the heaviness of your arms and legs on the bed.

betrayal.text: “We support you,” “you can count on us” — Sara Ahmed studied how such phrases are uttered in organizations and do nothing, and called them “non-performatives” (On Being Included, 2012). When you are betrayed, what collapses is not only trust in a person but the sense that the world is something you can lean on. Ahmed wrote about organizations, but if we extend her thought, betrayal in a personal relationship is a promise that was spoken and not kept. The pain of it is especially sharp because you oriented yourself by those words and built your life on them. Your pain is not naivety but evidence that you trusted. And that trust was not a mistake but a capacity worth keeping for those who deserve it.
betrayal.practice: Think of one person whose words and deeds match in your life, and tell them something warm today — even in a single message.

jealousy.text: One notification on someone else’s screen — and within a split second your chest is burning: Massumi showed that affect arrives in the body before we can think it over. Jealousy is a very human feeling, the fear of losing someone dear. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed shows how love can turn into fear and hostility when it seems that a beloved object is threatened by a third party. The feeling starts to “stick” to that figure. Jealousy is neither proof of infidelity nor a sign that you are rotten, but love mixed with the fear of loss. If you notice how quickly and bodily it arises, you can give yourself a pause before acting: the wave does not have to become a deed.
jealousy.practice: When a pang of jealousy comes, place your hand where you feel it and take three slow breaths before doing anything.

resentment.text: Files of complaints that never reached anyone lie in cabinets for years — Sara Ahmed gathered such stories for her book Complaint! (2021). A long-held grievance is heavy, and it cannot be let go on command. Ahmed studied what happens to complaints that are not heard. She shows that they do not disappear but get “stuck” — in bodies, in files, in the corridors of institutions. People keep carrying them for years because there was nowhere to take them. Resentment is often a complaint that found no listener. Its long life is not your pettiness but a sign that it was never taken seriously. Ahmed also speaks of a “feminist ear” — the capacity to hear what usually goes unheard. Sometimes resentment eases when someone finally hears it — even if that someone is you.
resentment.practice: Write your grievance down as a complaint: what happened, what was violated, what you couldn’t say at the time. Read it aloud to yourself, like a friend who believes you.

heartbreak.text: Love, for Sara Ahmed, is an orientation: we turn toward a person and build our days, routes and habits around them. That is why, when your heart is broken, your whole body literally hurts, and it takes time. When a relationship ends, the direction you were turned toward disappears, and for a while the world loses its shape. Besides, feelings “stick” to things: a song, a café, a street remain soaked in a shared past and unexpectedly wound you. Your pain is not weakness but a reflection of how strongly you were oriented toward this person. Ahmed also writes about “reorientation”: gradually the body learns to turn toward new things. This does not happen quickly, and there is no need to rush yourself.
heartbreak.practice: Notice one thing that is “sticking” to the past right now and hurts. You don’t need to get rid of it — just name it and let it be for now.

impostor.text: Space invaders: that is what the sociologist Nirmal Puwar, and Sara Ahmed after her, call those who end up in places not originally designed for them. The fear that you are about to be exposed is agonizing, and many very capable people know it — especially them. The mismatch can be one of gender, background, class, age. Such people often feel that their presence is in question, even when they are doing everything well. Feeling like an impostor is often not knowledge of your incompetence but a sense of not matching the “norm” of a space that was set before you arrived. This is not your fault. Ahmed shows that your very presence in such places already changes them — and makes them a little more open to others.
impostor.practice: Say out loud to yourself one thing you see or can do differently precisely because you are “unlike” the typical person in your environment.

self_hatred.text: The words your inner critic scolds you with were rarely invented by you: Sara Ahmed shows that hate circulates in society, is passed from some to others and “sticks” to certain bodies. When that voice says you are bad and worthless, it hurts a great deal — but its verdict is not the truth about you. Self-hatred is often not your own discovery about yourself but internalized disdain that was once directed at you, or at people like you, and then stuck from within. Ahmed emphasizes that what has stuck can be noticed and gradually separated. The critic’s voice sounds like yours, but its words have often come from somewhere else. You don’t have to keep passing them on.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one of the inner critic’s phrases and ask: where did I first hear something like this? Is this voice really mine?

helplessness.text: Books, things that sustain you, time, humor, your body, people who understand — this is how Sara Ahmed, in Living a Feminist Life, assembles a “survival kit” for those who have come up against insurmountable walls. Powerlessness is hard to bear, especially when you are trying very hard. Massumi, drawing on Spinoza, defines affect as the capacity to affect and to be affected. This matters: even when you can do almost nothing, your capacity to be affected is not a weakness — it too is a form of participation in the world. When you can’t change everything, you can gather what helps you hold on. This is not surrender but a way of keeping yourself for the moment when change becomes possible.
helplessness.practice: Assemble your “survival kit” for real: put one book and one comforting object beside you, and keep at hand the number of one person who understands.

procrastination.text: In Queer Phenomenology Sara Ahmed looks long and hard at Husserl’s writing table: to write, the table has to be near and everything else behind your back. When you can’t get started even though you really need to, it’s easy to start berating yourself. Massumi writes that every action begins not with a decision but with a barely noticeable bodily movement — an “incipient tendency” that has not yet taken shape as an act. Ahmed adds that we more easily do what is within reach and what we are already turned toward. Procrastination is not laziness but a situation in which the task is “out of reach”: too big, frightening, or unconnected with where your body is turned. Instead of pressuring yourself, you can bring the task closer — lay out the materials, open the file — and let a tiny movement become a beginning.
procrastination.practice: Make the task “reachable”: put the thing you need in front of you or open the file. Nothing more is required — just stay near it for a minute.

uprooted.text: The smell of other people’s cooking, light switches at the wrong height, a language you can’t joke in — for Sara Ahmed, home is made of such small things as much as of walls. After emigration or a move the world around you may seem not to recognize you, and the old world is gone. Ahmed and colleagues edited the collection Uprootings/Regroundings (2003) on migration and home, and in Strange Encounters (2000) she wrote about how we come to be perceived as “strangers.” Home, for Ahmed, is what you were oriented toward. In a new place this orientation is lost, and the body literally doesn’t know which way to turn. Your disorientation is a normal response to losing a familiar orientation. Home is not simply lost; it is also created anew — through new habits, connections, and people who also know what it’s like to be “not from here.”
uprooted.practice: Choose one small habit from your former life — a dish, a song, a walk at a certain time — and repeat it in your new place this week.

overload.text: In “The Autonomy of Affect” Massumi retells an experiment: children were shown a short film about a melting snowman, and they rated the saddest scenes as the most pleasant. Intensity, he explained, lives apart from meaning — and the feed, notifications and news exhaust you in exactly this way, not because you can’t “cope.” Media, for Massumi, act on us primarily through intensity rather than content: tone, rhythm and image touch the body before we grasp the meaning. So the feed acts on the nervous system as a stream of small blows, even when it communicates nothing important. Feed fatigue is not a whim but the reaction of a body taking on too much intensity at once. It is not obliged to withstand an endless stream. Sometimes the wisest thing is to remove the source for a while and let the nervous system return to its own rhythm.
overload.practice: Put your phone face down for five minutes and just sit. Mark the moment when your shoulders and breathing became even a little quieter.

unreality.text: Half a second — that, for Massumi, is roughly how far consciousness lags behind the body. Usually the gap goes unnoticed, but sometimes it seems to stretch, and then the world, or you yourself, feel not quite real; this can be frightening and disorienting. In Queer Phenomenology, Sara Ahmed describes moments of disorientation when the world seems to “slip” and appears at a strange angle: the familiar suddenly stops being familiar. Life then feels as if it is happening behind glass. The feeling of unreality is an experience of a particular position between body and world, not proof that the world has vanished. The body goes on living and sensing. The gentle way back is through the simplest sensations it responds to.
unreality.practice: Take something warm or cold in your palms — a mug, a stone, a damp towel — and slowly name to yourself five qualities of what your fingers feel.

awe.text: Wonder, for Sara Ahmed in The Cultural Politics of Emotion, is a special emotion: the world suddenly appears as if you were seeing it for the first time. Awe before something vast or beautiful is its rare and precious form. For her, wonder is also a way of seeing that the world could have been otherwise and at some point became what it is. Massumi would describe awe as an intensity that exceeds any capacity to name it: the body is seized before words appear. Awe is not something to explain or immediately photograph. It is a moment when the capacity to be affected expands to its limit. You can simply live it and let it change you.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for one more minute without words. Then ask: what am I seeing now as if for the first time?

relief.text: Sinking into an old armchair so that you can’t tell where your body ends and the furniture begins — this is how Sara Ahmed describes comfort. When tension finally lets go, it is worth savoring. You held on for a long time — now you can breathe out with your whole body. Relief is the moment when the body can sink like that again after a long period of holding itself together. Massumi would emphasize that this is above all a bodily event: muscles, breath and heart change rhythm before we say “thank God.” Relief is worth not only realizing but living through the body, letting it relax completely. It shows how much strength went into the tension — and reminds you that the body knows how to let go.
relief.practice: Let your body “sink” into what supports it — a chair, a bed, the floor. Notice which muscles have let go, and stay like this for a minute.

calm.text: The table, the chair, the familiar room — in Queer Phenomenology Sara Ahmed calls such things the “background”: they recede so that we can attend to other things. Calm is an infrequent guest, and it is good to cherish it. Usually the background goes unnoticed until something disturbs it. Calm is a state in which the background can remain background, nothing demands urgent attention and the world feels reliable. Massumi would call it a time when intensity is quiet and even and the body is not mobilized. Calm doesn’t have to turn into productivity. You can simply be in it and notice what usually slips away: the quiet of the room, the light, your own breath.
calm.practice: Notice one thing from the “background” around you — a wall, the light, a sound outside the window — and stay with it for a minute, doing nothing else.

inspiration.text: Thought and sensation have not yet separated, and something is only beginning to take shape — Massumi calls this “thinking-feeling.” Something new seems to be asking to come out on its own, and it is a joyful state. He writes about it in Semblance and Event (2011). It is not a plan but an incipient tendency full of possibility. Sara Ahmed speaks of “desire lines” — paths that people tread themselves, bypassing the paved routes. Inspiration is the moment when you sense such a new path without yet knowing where it leads. It doesn’t need to be turned into a result right away. Let yourself walk a few steps along it — just to feel how the world changes when you walk differently.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down the way it came — without structuring or judging it. Notice where in your body you feel this inspiration.

schadenfreude.text: Envy, irritation, anxiety — Sianne Ngai collected such feelings in her book Ugly Feelings (2005) and studied them without moralizing. A prick of pleasure at someone else’s failure, hidden even from oneself, could easily belong to her collection. For Ngai, such feelings offer neither catharsis nor a sense of being in the right, and they often arise where a person has little opportunity to act: movement seems blocked. Schadenfreude is also like an “ugly feeling”: a tiny compensation for the sense that you yourself are stuck while someone else’s success weighs on you. This feeling does not define you. Rather, it points to a place where you lack movement. If you notice it without shame, you can ask: what do I want for myself?
schadenfreude.practice: Recall a moment of schadenfreude and ask yourself quietly: where in my life is movement blocked right now? One answer is enough.

contempt.text: A wrinkled nose, a head turned away: the psychologist Silvan Tomkins, whose ideas affect theory draws on, singled out this reaction to bad smells as a distinct affect and called it “dissmell” — we pull back, not letting something come closer. Contempt is hard to admit, with its coldness and superiority, but its nature is the same — bodily. Contempt, for Tomkins, is related to this gesture: it is a way of keeping another at a distance. Sara Ahmed adds that such feelings draw boundaries between “us” and “them.” Your contempt is above all a signal: something in this person feels like a threat to your order, your values or your peace. There is no need to reproach yourself for it. You can ask: what am I protecting myself from by pulling away — and do I need that distance?
contempt.practice: Notice what contempt looks like in your body: pressed lips, a raised chin, an averted gaze? Gently relax your face and see what remains of the feeling.

disgust.text: For something to disgust us, it first has to come too close — Sara Ahmed builds her chapter on disgust in The Cultural Politics of Emotion on this paradox. You want to recoil from a person, a situation, sometimes from yourself: it is a very bodily feeling. In pushing it away, we also draw a boundary: “this is not me.” Ahmed stresses that these boundaries are not natural: culture teaches us what to consider disgusting, and such judgments often “stick” to whole groups of people. Disgust is the work of a boundary, not an objective truth about what provokes it. This matters especially when disgust is directed at yourself: it may be an echo of other people’s judgments. You can question it rather than take it on faith.
disgust.practice: Name what disgusts you and ask yourself: how did I learn that this is “disgusting”? Think about whose voice that might have been.

revenge.text: A surge and a plot — that is a rough way to put the distinction Brian Massumi draws between affect and emotion. After an injury a wave rises, and a revenge plot already sounds in it: you were hurt. Affect is bodily intensity, a surge that arises before thought; emotion is what it takes shape as once it gets a name and a plot. Intensity, for Massumi, is always richer than any form: it holds many possible continuations, and only one of them becomes action. The thirst for revenge is one of the plots into which your strength might be cast, but far from the only one. The same energy can become a resolve to protect yourself, to name an injustice, to draw a boundary. There is no need to deny the rage. You can give it time and notice what other paths it opens — without harming anyone.
revenge.practice: Feel where in your body this rage lives, and take a few slow exhales. Then imagine three different actions this energy could turn into — none of which harms anyone.

anger_at_loved.text: A family photo where everyone is smiling is, for Sara Ahmed, the model “happy object”: warmth, harmony and joy are expected of a family in advance. So anger at a partner, parents or children feels like one of the most shameful feelings, although it is one of the most ordinary. Anger within a family feels like breaking the rules, and whoever feels it seems like the destroyer of the shared harmony. Ahmed notes that behind this picture there is often an unequal burden: someone is constantly giving way, caring, keeping quiet so that everyone can feel “fine.” Your anger may be reporting a real problem — exhaustion, an unfair distribution of care, unspoken hurts. This is no reason to lash out at your loved ones. But it is no reason to consider yourself a monster either: anger is a signal worth hearing.
anger_at_loved.practice: Write down one thing you do in your family “so that everyone feels fine” that wears you out. You don’t need to change anything right away — just name it.

ambivalence.text: An infant first divides the world into “good” and “bad,” and only later realizes that the mother who soothes and the mother who refuses are one and the same person: this is how Melanie Klein described feelings growing up. Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is a very common combination, although it is rarely spoken of aloud. Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, one of the founders of affect theory, drew here on the psychoanalyst Melanie Klein. Klein called this turn the “depressive position.” Sedgwick linked this position to “reparativeness,” the capacity to repair: to assemble a whole out of contradictory parts. Your ambivalence is not a breakdown of love but a sign of a mature view. You don’t have to choose one feeling. You can hold both, and that holding is itself already the work of repair.
ambivalence.practice: Draw a circle and put two dots inside it: one for what you love in this person, the other for what is hard to bear. Look: both are inside one circle.

guilty_relief.text: Being sad at a wedding, not crying at a funeral — Sara Ahmed calls a person who feels “the wrong thing” an “affect alien.” Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one often makes you such an alien too: how can I feel lightness if I love? Culture hands out scripts of correct feelings, and deviating from them feels like guilt. But, for Ahmed, such mismatches are common and honestly tell us a lot about our lives. Your relief is not a betrayal of love but the body’s response to the end of a long strain. Love and relief do not cancel each other out. You can grieve and at the same time feel that it has become easier to breathe.
guilty_relief.practice: Take a few calm breaths and say to yourself: “I feel lighter — and I still love.” Notice how your body responds to these words.

indifference.text: Stuplimity: Sianne Ngai wove this word from “stupor” and “the sublime” to describe how shock and boredom mix and sensitivity goes dull when impressions are too many and keep repeating. Sometimes, where something “should” move you, there is emptiness, and this is frightening: do I really not care? Ngai stresses that this is not an absence of feeling but a particular form of it — a response to being overfull. Your indifference may be not coldness but protection: the psyche muffles the signal because there is too much of it. Massumi would add that affect keeps acting in the body even when it hasn’t taken shape as an emotion. The feeling may return later, in quiet. There is no need to squeeze it out of yourself.
indifference.practice: Put away all news and feeds for five minutes and listen to your body: has anything changed — even tiredness, even warmth?

escape.text: Sooner or later a diagonal path gets worn across any city lawn — where people actually find it easier to walk. Sara Ahmed calls such paths “desire lines,” and the urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a familiar role — can resemble them: sudden and strong. This is about the wish to change your circumstances, not to leave life. In Queer Phenomenology she writes about the lines along which we move: life often follows well-trodden paths, and the more people have walked them, the more natural they seem. The wish to escape is a sign that your path may not run where the road has been laid. It is neither a whim nor weakness. You don’t have to take off immediately. But it is worth noticing where your own path is pulling — and taking at least a small step along it.
escape.practice: On your next walk, turn where you feel drawn rather than where the path leads — even for just one block. Notice what your body feels on this “desire line.”

forbidden_attraction.text: A straight line, for Sara Ahmed, is not nature but habit, worn down by many who came before us. Attraction to the “wrong” or an unavailable person is embarrassing and confusing, but affect theory passes no moral verdict on it. In Queer Phenomenology Ahmed writes that desire is an orientation: we turn toward some objects and away from others. But what ends up “within reach” is largely set in advance — by habits, norms, the paths we have walked. That is why desire directed “the wrong way” feels like a malfunction. Ahmed, however, shows that deviations from straight lines are part of how living bodies move through the world. Such attraction speaks of a living turn in you — toward something you are lacking right now. You don’t need to decide right away what to do with it. You can ask yourself what exactly you have turned toward.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Name to yourself in one word the quality that draws you to this person. Then look around: where else in your life is there at least a trace of it?

social_anxiety.text: “Just don’t worry” is advice that never works, and Brian Massumi explains why: in the essay “The Autonomy of Affect” he shows that the body reacts before consciousness. Your cheeks burn, your throat goes dry, your heart pounds before you have thought anything about being judged. Massumi calls affect “autonomous”: it does not obey the will directly. Your reaction is not foolishness or weakness of character but the fast work of a body responding to the presence of others. There is no need to be ashamed of it. You can let the wave pass and notice: the nervousness is there, but it is not all that is in me. Others most likely see it much less than you think.
social_anxiety.practice: In a moment of nervousness, feel your feet on the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Tell yourself: “My body got there before me — and that’s allowed.”

uncertainty.text: Someone laughs in a queue, the wind shifts, a neighbor’s window lights up — the anthropologist Kathleen Stewart builds her book Ordinary Affects (2007) from such small things. You don’t know what will happen; it’s exhausting, and you long for some clarity. Stewart, close to affect theory, describes everyday life as a flow in which something is always emerging, shifting, beginning. In her view, ordinary life consists not of clear plans but of many small events that are felt by the body before they come together into a story. Stewart urges us to notice these small shifts, not just wait for a big answer. Uncertainty is not only an anxious void but also a living “something is happening,” in which good things are possible too. This doesn’t require you to “reframe your anxiety positively.” But you can shift your attention from the vast unknown to the small thing that is already happening now.
uncertainty.practice: Look out the window or step outside for a couple of minutes and note three small events: a sound, a movement, a change in the weather. This too is the future, already happening.

waiting.text: Hope, for Brian Massumi, is not confidence in a good outcome but a sense of openness present in any “now”; that is how he puts it in the interviews collected in Politics of Affect (2015). Waiting for an answer, results, news is painful: all your attention is turned toward a moment that has not yet arrived. Massumi doesn’t promise the answer will be good; he invites you to notice that life doesn’t go on pause while you wait. When we are wholly directed toward a future answer, the present shrinks to an empty gap. Waiting is easier if you bring your attention back to the present — not to distract yourself but to see that life is going on now too. The result will come when it comes. And this moment is already here.
waiting.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and simply notice what is happening around you: sounds, light, sensations in your body. There is no answer yet — but you do have these two minutes.

regret.text: Paranoid reading hunts for the hidden catch; reparative reading looks for what can still be mended. Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick distinguished these two positions — toward texts and, in effect, toward life. Regret that circles round — “if only I had…” — reads the past the first way. The “paranoid” one strives to foresee everything and protect itself in advance from bad surprises; it endlessly double-checks what went wrong. The “reparative” one allows itself to hope: it acknowledges that the future may differ from the present — and therefore that the past could have turned out differently too. It sounds paradoxical, but it is freeing: back then you acted in concrete circumstances, not according to an inevitable law. Regret doesn’t have to become a self-trial. It can be turned into care — for what can still be repaired, and for the version of yourself that went through all this.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and then one small “reparative” action that is possible now: a word, a letter, care for yourself or for someone else.

quote.text: …it is also possible for her to entertain such profoundly painful, profoundly relieving, ethically crucial possibilities as that the past, in turn, could have happened differently from the way it actually did.
quote.author: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick
quote.source: “Paranoid Reading and Reparative Reading,” in Touching Feeling (2003)

longing.text: Impression — both a feeling and an imprint, a trace on a surface: in The Cultural Politics of Emotion Sara Ahmed uses both senses. Your longing is a feeling with a face, a voice, a smell. Other people, for Ahmed, literally leave impressions on us: their presence shapes our habits, gestures, the way we move through the world. When the person is not near, the impression remains — and aches, like a place where something is missing. Your longing is neither weakness nor dependence but evidence of how deeply you were touched. The impression doesn’t need to be erased. Over time it can become not a wound but a part of you that you carry with care.
longing.practice: Notice one habit, gesture or turn of phrase of yours that came from this person. Let yourself smile at this trace, even if it is sad.

world_pain.text: No one can feel another’s pain exactly as they feel it — Sara Ahmed opens her chapter on pain in The Cultural Politics of Emotion with this admission. And yet pain for those who suffer from wars, violence and injustice can be almost physical, especially when the news keeps pouring in. For Ahmed, not being able to fully know another’s pain does not justify indifference: ethics consists in allowing ourselves to be affected by what we cannot fully know. Ahmed also warns of something else: compassion should not turn someone else’s pain into a story about ourselves. Your pain is a sign of openness to the world, and it is valuable. But you don’t have to carry it alone and without a break. You can let yourself feel — and look for concrete ways, within your means, to stand by those who are struggling.
world_pain.practice: Place your hand on your chest and say: “I cannot know this pain fully, but I do not turn it away.” Then choose one small, concrete act of support.

rejection.text: A stranger, for Sara Ahmed, is not someone we don’t know but someone we recognize as “out of place”: this is the subject of her book Strange Encounters (2000). When you weren’t accepted into a circle, weren’t chosen, were turned away from, it wounds deeply. The boundary between “us” and “strangers” is created by the group itself, by its habits and expectations, not by the qualities of the person rejected. Rejection says more about how that circle is arranged than about your worth. The pain doesn’t disappear because of this, and it shouldn’t be minimized: we all need to belong. But you don’t have to accept someone else’s boundary as a verdict on yourself — and you can look for places where you are not a “stranger” but one of their own.
rejection.practice: Call or drop in where you feel “in place” — a person, a group, a familiar café. Even for just a few minutes.

abandonment.text: A knot in a net: that is how Brian Massumi suggests we picture a person — not a closed unit but a crossing of many connections. Hence the fear of being abandoned, one of the most ancient: without others, no one survives. Massumi stresses that affect is always about relationships. In an interview from Politics of Affect, he describes affect as our participation in processes larger than ourselves, and says that strong feelings sharpen our sense of being woven into life, of belonging to other people and places. That is why the threat of losing someone close is perceived by the body as a threat to our very footing, even if the mind understands that you will cope. Your fear is not an exaggeration but a sensitivity to how much connections mean to you. But the field of relationships is always wider than one person. You can notice the other threads that hold you too — even thin ones.
abandonment.practice: Go through your threads in your mind — people, places, activities, animals, habits — and fold down a finger for each. Look at your hand: more than one thread is holding you.

unrequited.text: In loving another, we often also love an image of ourselves beside them — Sara Ahmed takes up this idea of Freud’s in The Cultural Politics of Emotion. That is what makes unrequited love hurt in a particular way: the feeling is real, but it goes unanswered. So unrequitedness wounds twice over: there is no answer from the person, and this ideal image of ourselves seems to collapse. Part of your pain is about a lost future you had already imagined. This is not naivety: this is how love works. That image may also say something about what you want for yourself. You can keep it and look for other paths toward it — not only through this person.
unrequited.practice: Write down how you saw yourself beside this person. Choose one trait from this image that you can develop without them.

humiliation.text: A burning face, eyes on the floor — Silvan Tomkins saw in this not a sign of worthlessness but the trace of an interrupted interest in people. After humiliation you want to hide, lower your eyes, leave the room. Tomkins, whose ideas Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick rediscovered for the humanities, combined shame and humiliation into a single affect — “shame-humiliation.” For Tomkins, it arises not when we don’t care but when interest or joy is interrupted without being extinguished: we were reaching toward people, toward recognition, and the connection was suddenly broken. Your humiliation speaks not of your worthlessness but of how much connection with people matters to you. Sedgwick emphasized that shame is deeply social and contagious: it often belongs more to the situation than to you. You can remind yourself: I needed contact, and there is nothing shameful in that.
humiliation.practice: Place your palm on your chest, as if comforting someone dear to you, and tell yourself: “I needed contact. There is nothing shameful in that.”

body_shame.text: Doorways, airplane seats, sizes in shops — spaces, for Sara Ahmed, “take the shape” of some bodies in advance and not of others. If you are unhappy with your body, it is not your personal fault. Ahmed writes about “comfort”: to be comfortable is to feel so at ease in your surroundings that the boundary between body and world almost disappears. But this is not so for every body. If your body does not match that shape, you get the sense that it is “wrong,” although the problem is the narrowness of the frame. Your dissatisfaction is largely a trace of these norms, not the truth about you. Ahmed does not call on you to love yourself urgently. But you can notice where your body feels freer — and gradually choose more such places, people and activities.
body_shame.practice: Recall a place or situation where your body feels free and not under evaluation. What is different there? Could you spend at least a little time there today?

illness.text: “No one has yet determined what a body can do,” Spinoza wrote, and Deleuze and Massumi like to repeat the phrase. When the body lets you down and your familiar trust in it collapses, fear, anger and exhaustion are legitimate here. For them, the body is not a machine that is either working or broken but a process, a capacity to affect and to be affected. This capacity changes: illness narrows some possibilities, but the body keeps searching for others — a different rhythm, different supports, different joys. Illness does not cancel you: you remain a living field of relationships in which more than suffering is possible. This is no reason to demand resilience of yourself. Rather, it is an invitation to notice small changes — moments when things get a little easier — and to lean on them.
illness.practice: Note one moment today when your body felt even a little easier or more pleasant: warm tea, light, a comfortable position. Stay in it for a few breaths.

pride.text: Shame makes you hide your face, pride lets you show it — Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, following Silvan Tomkins, wrote about how closely these two affects are linked. Pride in what you have done is a good feeling, and there is no need to hide it out of modesty. Tomkins considered the positive affects — interest and joy — not a pleasant addition to life but something worth consciously sustaining: they nourish curiosity and the capacity to act. Spinoza, from whose philosophy affect theory grew, called “self-contentment” the joy that arises when a person contemplates themselves and their own power of acting. Your pride is not vanity but an opportunity to see your strength and not apologize for it. You can savor this joy without hurrying.
pride.practice: Tell someone about what you managed to do, without caveats like “it’s nothing special.” Notice how this feels in your body.

melancholy.text: The “melancholic migrant,” reproached for holding on to what was lost, is one of the figures Sara Ahmed defends in The Promise of Happiness. Your bright sadness, where sorrow lives alongside tenderness, deserves the same defense: it needs neither to be driven away nor treated. Ahmed criticizes a culture that demands that we absolutely “be happy” and hurries us to “let go” of the past. She defends the right not to hurry. Ahmed also speaks of “the freedom to be unhappy”: the right to feelings that don’t fit into mandatory optimism. Your melancholy is not a mood error but a way of gently holding on to what mattered. It doesn’t need fixing. You can simply listen to what exactly it remembers.
melancholy.practice: Sit with this mood for a couple of minutes without changing anything. If you like, name quietly one thing it seems to be keeping safe in memory.
